plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: The 'This computer' section. Exact versions, tools, stand-ins for what the machine lacks and the rules for sharing it meant I could test the required stack here before writing a plan, instead of guessing, and that turned up failures no plan written from memory would have caught. I also liked the clean split between what is fixed (Three.js r180, WebGPU, ink filter, Rapier 0.19.3, audio rules, 10-foot UX) and what is left to judgement (genre, camera, research, effort). Putting performance out of scope removed a common reason for timid design.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Three things. (1) 'Multiplayer ... into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own': the hub README says a game outside a session is simply unaffected, so I could not tell whether standalone multiplayer is wanted. I planned local split-screen co-op as the answer, but that is my reading. (2) 'The engine's native style' and 'the engine's asset library': three.js has neither a house style nor an asset library, so I read them as its toon materials and built-in geometries. (3) The WebGPU flags: with the three listed, the device is lost right after the first render while a frame counter keeps climbing, and screenshots stay blank. The five-flag list in the hub's own check script works. A smaller one: the hub repo's lib/kit targets three.js r186 and Rapier 0.20, which conflicts with the versions asked for unless you notice that the link points only at lib/hub.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Sizing the scope for builders I cannot see or answer. The brief asks for a complete demo showing every mechanic with no stubs, the source's appeal is constant variety, and the plan has to work in one run with no follow-up questions, whatever the builder's strength. Settling on 16 zones and 4 bosses, with the rule 'make it shorter, never thinner' and a feature list a test can enforce, took the most thought. Close behind was keeping how the source plays while making every name, character, level, line and look original.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: Put the five-flag WebGPU launch line in the 'This computer' section. Say in one sentence whether multiplayer is expected outside a hub session. Reword the art and animation lines for engines with no asset library or house style, for example 'build on the engine's own materials and animation system'. Link the raw hub README and say which client version is current. Tell the planner how capable the builders are and roughly how long the demo should play, because both decide the scope more than anything else in the brief.
